messages.author: 0227543d81e2924c
messages.subject: naive question
parts:
So, any number of methods for working with 'unmarked' animals often make the explicit assumption that an 'encountered' individual is not 'counted' >1 times (what one of my colleagues calls the 'classical conceit of the hot-shot field biologist who would never do that' - said colleague being more cynical than me). 

Since distance sampling often falls under the larger umbrella of 'analysis of data from unmarked individiauls', was wondering if someone would point me at the canonical reference(s) for the analysis of the impact of the violation of this assumption on interesting things -- like (say) abundance (where even a naive assessment would suggest that >1 counts for some fraction of individuals would lead to a positive bias in N. I'm particular interested in how distance sampling congensceti would 'test' for a violation of this assumption (as opposed to the distance sampling diletante who might simply assume it never happens).

Cheers...

messages.author: 9b03386432b784c0
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] naive question
parts:
Hi Evan,

The truth is that even a distance sampling diletante ;) - hey... I wonder if that is what I should add to my CV now... - does not need assume it never happens, it can happen and cause no problem whatsoever. You must need common sense to evaluate if it is a problem or not in a given scenario.

Imagine the situation where you cover the same transects 10 times, one time in each of 10 days. If you pool the data in the right way, you can still estimate an average density over the 10 days. You might actually have seen more animals than the number of animals you estimate to be there. But there's no problem about it. The point estimate and the corresponding variance of density can be obtained.

Random movement across lines will not matter either. For any animal you spot again in the next transect because the animal happened moved that way will on average be cancelled by an animal that was in transect 2 when you were going over transect 1 and moved to transect 1 when you were covering transect 2.

The real problem will occur if you drive animals from one transect to the next and them keep counting the same animal over and over again. Or if say you are surveying an area over which animals are migrating and the migration is not independent of the transect placement, say.

Does that help?

cheers

Tiago

messages.author: f2122b34f1aa6e95
messages.subject: Re: [distance-sampling] naive question
parts:
Evan

To amplify what Tiago has said, the distance sampling assumption at issue in your question is "objects are detected at their initial location", hence about animal movement rather than about double counting.

The first paragraph of Section 2.1.2 of Buckland et al. (2001) would be a first port of call.  As to a "test" of animal movement, Figure 2.2 of same reference provides a qualitative measure of responsive movement (not double counting).

Distance sampling methods that incorporate the effect of movement are under development, beginning with an assessment of bias induced by movement developed by Glennie et al. (2015) PLoS ONE https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0121333

messages.author: 1fb54f491646a589
messages.subject: RE: [distance-sampling] naive question
parts:
Following up on Tiago’s comments, you can think of distance sampling as being a form of plot sampling where we estimate the proportion of animals detected on the plot.  So the effective size of the plot is this proportion multiplied by the actual size.  There is no reason why the effective sizes of the plots, when all added together, can’t exceed the size of the study area.  When that occurs, of course your sample size exceeds the population size.  There is a violation of the independence assumption, but given good survey design, coupled with variance estimation methods that are robust to failures of this assumption, the implications are mild.  In my 2006 Auk paper, I showed by simulation that for a point transect survey in which each bird is expected to be detected from on average between 3 and 4 points, bias was just one half of one percent, even though the number of detections far exceeded the population size.

 

Steve Buckland
